questions.q: Why could Newton write down the law of universal gravitation but never calculate the mass of the Earth?
options: He lacked an accurate value for the radius of the Earth, which was only measured much later
Every gravitational measurement he could make gave only the product of big G and the Earth's mass — two unknowns tangled together that he could not separate
His law was only an approximation that broke down for objects as large as a planet
He had no way to measure the gravitational field strength at the Earth's surface
questions.explanation: In Newton's day the Earth was always one of the two masses in any gravity measurement, so observations like the Moon's orbit only pinned down the product (big G times the Earth's mass). A single equation with two unknowns cannot be solved. The Earth's radius was actually known since antiquity, so that option is the tempting distractor.

questions.q: What second, independent measurement was needed to finally separate big G from the mass of the Earth?
options: A more precise measurement of the Moon's orbit over a longer baseline
The gravitational attraction between two ordinary laboratory masses, in a situation where the Earth is not involved at all
The weight of a known mass measured at the top of a tall mountain
The time a ball takes to fall a known distance near the surface
questions.explanation: Measuring the tiny pull between two known lab masses gives big G directly, with the Earth left out entirely. Once G is known on its own, you divide it out of Newton's tangled product (G times the Earth's mass) and the Earth's mass falls out.

questions.q: In the torsion balance, why is it essential that the suspending wire resists twisting only very weakly?
options: A weak wire lets the rod swing faster, so trials finish more quickly
A feeble restoring force means even the minuscule gravitational pull on the small balls produces a twist large enough to measure
A weak wire reduces the heat generated by friction in the apparatus
A weak wire makes the apparatus lighter and easier to move with pulleys
questions.explanation: Because a thin wire fights back so gently, a force far too small for any ordinary scale still twists it by a visible amount. The balance converts an almost non-existent force into a measurable rotation — a way of seeing the invisible.

questions.q: How did Cavendish determine the stiffness of the wire without ever applying a known force to it?
options: He hung known weights from the wire and measured how far it stretched
He let the rod oscillate freely and timed the period of its swing, since a stiffer wire snaps the rod back faster
He compared the wire to a standard wire of known stiffness held by the Royal Society
He calculated it from the chemical composition and diameter of the wire
questions.explanation: The period of the slow oscillation — about fifteen minutes per swing at first — depends directly on the wire's stiffness, a stiffer wire giving a quicker swing. By timing the swing, the rod effectively measured its own suspension, the masterstroke buried inside the experiment.

questions.q: When the great spheres were in place and the rod settled at its twisted equilibrium, what two effects were exactly in balance?
options: The weight of the rod and the buoyancy of the surrounding air
The gravitational pull turning the small balls toward the big ones, and the wire's restoring twist turning it back
Air pressure on one side of the sealed case and a partial vacuum on the other
The static charge on the balls and the gravitational pull of the Earth
questions.explanation: At rest the gravitational torque on the small balls exactly equals the wire's restoring torque. Knowing the wire's stiffness and seeing how far it had twisted, Cavendish could calculate the gravitational force — about 170 nanonewtons, the weight of a grain of sand.

questions.q: From memory: what steps did Cavendish take to stop his own presence and the environment from swamping such a tiny signal?
keyPoints: He realised his own body heat would create air currents, and that he himself even exerted a gravitational pull, so he removed himself from the room.
He sealed the apparatus in a large mahogany case to block draughts, and put that case inside a closed shed in his garden.
He moved the heavy spheres with ropes and pulleys from outside the shed, and read the tiny twist through telescopes mounted in the walls — never breathing on the instrument.
questions.explanation: The genius was discipline: Cavendish became a pair of distant eyes at a telescope watching a sealed box. If you recalled the body-heat / air-current threat and the remote operation by pulleys and telescopes, grade yourself Good or Easy.

questions.q: Using the modern data-sheet values, calculate the mass of the Earth from the gravitational field strength at its surface.
questions.explanation: Rearranging \(g = GM/r^{2}\) leaves the Earth's mass as the only unknown, because g, r and — thanks to Cavendish — G are all known. This is exactly the calculation any HSC student can do, and the number Newton could never reach.

questions.q: What did Henry Cavendish himself actually set out to measure in his 1798 paper?
options: The universal gravitational constant, big G
The density of the Earth — how tightly packed its material is compared with water
The mass of the Moon
The acceleration due to gravity at the surface
questions.explanation: The symbol big G does not appear anywhere in his work; it was not in common use until around 1873. His paper is titled 'Experiments to Determine the Density of the Earth', and he found the Earth is about 5.5 times denser than water.

questions.q: Cavendish found the Earth's average density to be about 5.5 times that of water, while surface rock is only about 2.5–3 times. What did this imply?
options: The Earth must be hollow at its centre
The interior of the Earth must be made of something much denser than rock, such as a metallic (iron) core
The measurement of surface rock density must have been wrong
Water must be far denser deep inside the Earth
questions.explanation: If the whole planet averages 5.5 but surface rock is only ~2.5–3, the inside must be much heavier than rock — the first real evidence of a dense metallic core. Seismic waves did not confirm this directly until the twentieth century.

questions.q: From memory: why does big G remain the most poorly known of the fundamental constants, even today?
keyPoints: Gravity is staggeringly weak — by far the weakest of the fundamental forces.

There is no gravity shield: unlike electric or magnetic fields, you cannot block gravity out, so the pull of the building, the experimenter, the water table and distant mountains all contaminate the measurement.
Modern torsion-balance measurements since about 1990 disagree with each other by more than their stated error bars — a hidden systematic error that almost every team has hit.
questions.explanation: The same brutal fact that made Cavendish's job so hard — gravity's weakness and the impossibility of shielding it — still limits us, leaving G uncertain at about 22 parts per million. If you recalled 'weak force, can't be shielded, results disagree', grade yourself Good or Easy.
